chunks: Muhammad ibn 'Ibad said: Musa ibn Yahya ibn Khalid informed me: Abu Ibrahim (peace be upon him) said to Yahya: 'O Abu Ali, I am dying; only a week remains for me. Keep my death secret and come to me on Friday at midday, and you and my friends pray for me individually. And observe when this tyrant travels to Ar-Raqqa and returns to Iraq; he should not see you and you should not see him, for my own sake, for I have seen in your star, the star of your son, and his star that he will come upon you, so beware of him.' Then he said: 'O Abu Ali, convey to him from me: Musa ibn Ja'far says to you: My messenger will come to you on Friday and inform you of what you see. And you will know tomorrow when you stand before Allah, who is the wrongdoer and the aggressor against his companion. And peace.' Yahya went out from his presence, his eyes reddened from weeping, until he entered upon Harun and informed him of his story and what he replied. Harun said to him: 'If he does not claim prophethood after a few days, how good our state will be!' When it was Friday, Abu Ibrahim (peace be upon him) died. Harun had already traveled to Al-Mada'in before that. He was brought out to the people so they could look at him, then he was buried (peace be upon him), and the people returned. They split into two groups: one group said: 'He died,' and the other group said: 'He did not die.'

key_terms.أَبُو إِبْرَاهِيمَ: Abu Ibrahim, a title for Imam Musa al-Kadim (peace be upon him)
key_terms.الرَّقَّة: Ar-Raqqa, a city in Syria where Harun traveled
key_terms.الزَّوَال: Midday, the time when the sun passes its zenith
key_terms.الطَّاغِيَةُ: The tyrant, referring to Harun al-Rashid

ai.seo_question: What were Imam Kadim's final instructions to Yahya regarding his death and Harun al-Rashid?
ai.summary: This narrative from Shaykh al-Tusi’s *Kitab al-Ghayba* highlights the strategic concealment of Imam Musa al-Kadim’s death to manage Abbasid surveillance, specifically noting the instruction to pray for him individually to avoid detection. It underscores the theological tension between the visible reality of martyrdom and the Shia belief in the Imam’s enduring presence, culminating in the division of the community into those who accepted his death and those who awaited his reappearance.
